questions.q: What is the local name for shifting cultivation in the northeastern states of India?
questions.a: The local name is "jhum" or "jhum cultivation". A wrong answer (e.g., "podu", "bewar", "kumri") reveals the student knows other regional names but cannot identify the specific term used in Northeast India, which is a frequent board exam question.

questions.q: Why do shifting cultivators abandon a field after 2-3 years of cultivation?
questions.a: Soil fertility declines rapidly because the nutrient store is in the biomass, not the soil; burning releases nutrients for a few crops, but without fertilizers, yields drop. A wrong answer like "because of weed infestation" or "because they own new land" shows misunderstanding of the nutrient cycle in tropical soils.

questions.q: On an outline map of India, mark and label three states where shifting cultivation (jhum) is predominantly practiced.
questions.a: Correct states: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram (also Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura). Steps: 1) Recall the northeastern hilly states. 2) Identify those with tribal populations practicing jhum. 3) Mark on map. A wrong answer marking central Indian states (e.g., Madhya Pradesh) confuses shifting cultivation with other tribal farming like "bewar" (which is also shifting but in different region) – but the question asks for jhum specifically.

questions.q: Compare the environmental impact of shifting cultivation with a long fallow period (15-20 years) versus a shortened fallow period (3-5 years) due to population pressure.
questions.a: Long fallow allows forest regeneration, soil recovery, and biodiversity maintenance; shortened fallow leads to soil degradation, erosion, loss of biodiversity, and conversion to grassland/scrub. A wrong answer that says both are equally harmful ignores the critical role of fallow length in sustainability.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the "Jhum Control Policy" of the Government of India in replacing shifting cultivation with settled agriculture in Northeast India.
questions.a: The policy has had limited success because it often ignores tribal land tenure systems, cultural practices, and lack of alternative livelihoods; settled agriculture on steep slopes without terracing can cause more erosion. A wrong answer claiming "complete success" or "total failure" shows lack of nuanced evaluation.

questions.q: Design a sustainable land-use plan for a hilly tribal village in Nagaland that reduces dependence on shifting cultivation while respecting traditional rights.
questions.a: A good plan includes: 1) Agroforestry with nitrogen-fixing trees, 2) Terracing on gentler slopes for permanent fields, 3) Community-managed fallow enrichment, 4) Off-farm income (handicrafts, tourism). A poor answer suggests only "ban shifting cultivation" or "give chemical fertilizers" without addressing slope, soil, and socio-cultural factors.
